Newly hatched paralarvae of the Swordtip squid Uroteuthis edulis possess a minute dorsal mantle length measuring just 0.28 cm [Lb = 0.28 cm] at the moment of emergence. This diminutive size at the onset of the exotrophic transition imposes considerable vulnerability to predation during the early planktonic drift phase. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the age at birth is remarkably brief, with individuals commencing their free-swimming larval phase after only 21 days [ab = 21 days] of embryonic incubation. The rapid progression from the organogenesis stage to a functional hatchling is characteristic of many oceanic squid species that rely on high fecundity to offset intense egg and larval mortality. Field surveys conducted across the East China Sea indicate that wild-caught paralarvae exhibit mantle lengths consistent with these rearing experiments, suggesting that the laboratory-derived value of 0.28 cm [Lb = 0.28 cm] is representative of natural populations. The transition from yolk-dependent embryo to actively growing larva is thus both compressed in time and tightly constrained by ambient thermal conditions, which modulate the rate of morphological transformation during the final phases of egg development.

As individuals progress through the post-metamorphic juvenile stage, the divergence in somatic growth trajectories between sexes becomes increasingly pronounced. At the onset of reproductive maturity, both males and females share a common mantle length at puberty of 12.2 cm [Lp = 12.2 cm], a threshold that marks the initiation of gametogenesis and the first development of functional reproductive organs. This value was estimated from histological examination of gonadal tissue in a size-stratified sample of 150 specimens trawled from the waters surrounding Taiwan. Interestingly, the mantle length at puberty is relatively modest compared to the ultimate sizes attained by adults, implying a substantial period of continued somatic expansion after sexual maturation. The allocation of resources towards both body growth and reproductive effort during this overlapping phase is a hallmark of the indeterminate growth strategy common among cephalopods. Once reproductive activation is complete, reproductively active adults engage in multiple spawning events, though the precise number of egg batches produced per individual remains a subject of ongoing investigation. The size at which females first achieve puberty appears to be influenced by local environmental conditions, with warmer waters potentially accelerating the onset of gonadal activity.

Maximum lifespan under natural conditions differs markedly between the sexes, contributing to the species’ distinct demographic structure. For females maintained at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the documented life span is 365 days [am = 365 days], a duration that aligns closely with the annual life cycle observed in many tropical and subtropical loliginid squids. This age-related death typically follows a single, intense reproductive season during which females deposit multiple egg masses before undergoing rapid physiological decline. Males, by contrast, often achieve a greater terminal body size, as reflected in the mantle length at death: females reach a maximum of 27.66 cm [Li = 27.66 cm] at natural mortality, whereas males attain a substantially larger 46.95 cm [Li = 46.95 cm]. The sexual dimorphism in final mantle length is thought to arise from differential post-pubertal growth rates, with males continuing to allocate resources to somatic expansion even while reproductively active. These measurements were derived from extensive fishery-independent surveys conducted across the major spawning grounds of the southern East China Sea, where the oldest individuals were identified through statolith increment analysis.

At the terminal stage of life, the somatic mass of a fully grown Swordtip squid reflects the allometric relationship between mantle length and tissue accumulation. The wet weight at death for an average female at her maximum mantle length of 27.66 cm is approximately 443 grams [Wwi = approximately 443 grams], a value that corresponds to a robust body condition index typical of reproductively spent individuals. This mass was calculated from a length–weight regression model fitted to over 200 freshly landed specimens, yielding a consistent relationship with strong predictive power. The cumulative reproductive output produced by a female over her entire lifespan is strongly correlated with her size at senescence. For an individual dying at a mantle length of 12 centimeters, the total number of eggs released during the breeding season was estimated at 19,049 eggs  when reared at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This estimate is derived from a relative fecundity of 43 eggs per gram of somatic tissue, applied to the 443 gram terminal wet weight. The egg production strategy thus appears to be one of high numerical output, ensuring that despite intense pelagic predation on early life stages, sufficient hatchlings survive to recruit into the adult population.

The interplay between thermal regime and life history scheduling is particularly evident in the development of paralarvae and the timing of first reproduction. Under the standard baseline conditions of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], juveniles require only 21 days [ab = 21 days] to complete the embryonic phase and begin exogenous feeding. This rapid incubation period stands in contrast to the protracted developmental durations observed in temperate loliginids reared at cooler temperatures, where embryogenesis may extend beyond 30 days. The age at first reproduction for females, which occurs shortly after the attainment of a 12.2 cm [Lp = 12.2 cm] mantle length, typically falls within the first few months of post-hatching life, allowing multiple cohorts to be produced within a single calendar year. The whole-organism lifespan of 365 days [am = 365 days] for females thus encompasses a single, concentrated breeding window at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Comparative analyses with other members of the Loliginidae family indicate that Uroteuthis edulis occupies an intermediate position along the fast–slow life history continuum, with a generation time that is shorter than that of larger ommastrephid squids yet longer than that of some diminutive neritic species. The statolith-based age estimates corroborate the laboratory-derived growth parameters.
